title: EPS: Earnings Per Share
subtitle: How much profit does each share held earn a shareholder?
openingQuestion: A company has Net Income of 200 billion, 100 million shares outstanding. What is the EPS?
explanation: Earnings per share converts a whole company's profit into the portion belonging to a single share, making it comparable against the market price. It's best to use the diluted version, which counts options and convertible bonds that could turn into shares, since that's the real denominator shareholders will end up sharing. Also remember this metric is affected by buybacks: a smaller denominator makes it rise even while profit stands still.

realWorldExample.description: Vinhomes's EPS can swing sharply between quarters due to how real-estate revenue is recognized at each project handover - investors need to look at annual EPS or the long-term trend rather than a single quarter to avoid drawing the wrong conclusion.

quiz.question: Why use diluted EPS instead of basic EPS?
options: Diluted EPS counts options/warrants - reflecting dilution risk
It's a mandatory disclosure with no independent analytical meaning
Basic EPS is calculated wrong because it doesn't remove treasury shares from the denominator
Diluted EPS is always higher than basic, so it looks better to shareholders
quiz.explanation: Diluted EPS shows what EPS would be if ALL options, warrants, and convertibles were exercised. It's usually lower than basic EPS. It reflects real dilution risk more accurately.

quiz.question: A company issues 20% more new shares to raise capital (without an immediate change in Net Income). What happens to EPS?
options: It's undetermined without information about the new shares' price
EPS doesn't change because Net Income stays the same as before
EPS rises because the company now has more capital to expand
EPS falls - the same Net Income divided by more shares
quiz.explanation: This is dilution: issuing more shares increases the denominator in EPS = Net Income / Shares, causing EPS to fall.

quiz.question: Net income is 480 billion, shares outstanding is 120 million. What is the EPS?
options: 25,000 dong (= 120 million ÷ 480 billion, numerator and denominator reversed)
400 dong (= 480 billion ÷ 1.2 billion, off by a zero)
4,000 dong (= 480 billion ÷ 120 million shares)
40,000 dong (= 480 billion ÷ 12 million, using the wrong share count)
quiz.explanation: EPS = Net Income / Shares Outstanding = 480,000,000,000 / 120,000,000 = 4,000 dong per share. Multiplying by the market P/E gives the theoretical price of that share.

quiz.question: EPS rises 15% but net income rises only 5%. What is the most likely cause?
options: The corporate tax rate was reduced during this period
The company just issued more shares to raise fresh capital
Gross margin improved thanks to lower input costs
The company bought back treasury shares, reducing shares outstanding
quiz.explanation: The numerator rose 5% while the result rose 15%, so the denominator must have shrunk. Treasury-share buybacks reduce shares outstanding, pushing EPS up without needing better business performance - a way of dressing up the metric worth recognizing.

quiz.question: Why isn't EPS alone enough to compare two businesses?
options: Because it depends on the number of shares, which varies by company
Because EPS doesn't account for a business's interest expense
Because EPS is only published annually, too infrequent for timely comparison
Because each industry applies its own separate EPS formula
quiz.explanation: A company could divide the same profit among 10 million or 1 billion shares, producing EPS figures a hundred times apart even though enterprise value hasn't changed. EPS is only meaningful when set beside the share price - that is, P/E.

keyTakeaways: EPS = Net Income / Diluted Shares Outstanding
Diluted EPS is more conservative, reflecting potential dilution

practicePrompt.question: A company has Net Income = 500 billion for the year, diluted shares outstanding = 100 million shares. What is this company's EPS (earnings per share)?
options: EPS = Net Income / Diluted Shares Outstanding = 500 billion / 100 million = 5,000 dong/share
EPS = 100 million / 500 billion, showing the number of shares corresponding to each dong of profit
EPS always equals the current share price trading on the exchange
EPS cannot be calculated without knowing the company's current share price on the market
practicePrompt.explanation: EPS = Net Income / Diluted Shares Outstanding = 500,000,000,000 / 100,000,000 = 5,000 dong/share. EPS is the foundation for calculating P/E (Price/EPS) - one of the most commonly used valuation metrics when comparing stocks.

application.title: Calculate EPS
application.message: Divide Net Income by Diluted Shares Outstanding for a listed company, then compare it against the EPS already published in that company's financial statements to check your calculation.
application.secondary: Diluted EPS is always more conservative than Basic EPS because it counts potential dilutive shares.

sections.text: EPS (Earnings Per Share) divides net profit by shares outstanding, answering the direct question every shareholder cares about: how much of the company's profit corresponds to each share I hold?

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: EPS = Net Income / Diluted Shares Outstanding.  **Example:** 200 billion / 100 million shares = 2,000 dong/share
Why use diluted EPS instead of basic EPS

Basic EPS only divides by shares actually outstanding. Diluted EPS is more conservative: it also counts stock options, warrants, and convertible bonds - if all these instruments were exercised, how many new shares would there be, and how much would EPS be diluted? Diluted EPS is almost always lower than or equal to basic EPS, and reflects the actual dilution risk existing shareholders face more accurately.
Dilution: when a falling EPS doesn't mean worse business

When a company issues 20% more new shares to raise capital, EPS falls immediately even though Net Income hasn't yet changed - because the same level of profit must now be divided among more shares. This is the dilution phenomenon, not a sign the company's business is deteriorating. Investors need to clearly distinguish between two causes of falling EPS: profit genuinely falling, or simply the denominator (share count) rising.

items: EPS can swing quarter to quarter due to how revenue is recognized (e.g. real estate handed over in stages) - look at the annual trend rather than a single quarter
P/E × EPS = theoretical share price under current market valuation
Diluted EPS is always more conservative - use it when assessing a company with many ESOPs or convertible bonds
Sustained EPS growth over many years is a far more positive signal than a single quarter's EPS spike

lines: EPS is the foundation block for calculating P/E - but always check whether an EPS rise or fall comes from real profit or from a change in share count.
